title: Union-Find
description: Build a disjoint-set class that merges groups, tests membership and counts the groups in near-constant time.
statement:
Build a `UnionFind` (disjoint-set) class that tracks which of `n` elements, numbered `0` to `n - 1`, belong to the same group. At the start every element is alone in its own group.

- `UnionFind(n)` creates `n` separate groups.
- `find(x)` returns the representative of `x`'s group: elements of the same group get the same value, elements of different groups get different values.
- `union(a, b)` merges the groups of `a` and `b`. It returns `True` if it joined two different groups and `False` if they were already one group (this includes `union(a, a)`).
- `connected(a, b)` says whether `a` and `b` are in the same group.
- `component_count()` returns the current number of groups.

**Example**

```python
groups = UnionFind(4)
groups.union(0, 1)           # True
groups.union(1, 0)           # False, already together
groups.connected(0, 1)       # True
groups.component_count()     # 3: the groups are {0, 1}, {2} and {3}
```

Aim for near-constant time per operation: the last tests make hundreds of thousands of calls.
tests:
other = UnionFind(7)
other.union(0, 1)
other.union(1, 2)
other.union(3, 4)
other.union(4, 5)
other.union(0, 3)
hints: Updating every member of a group on each union is slow. What if every element just pointed at a parent, and a group were named by the element at the top of its chain?
`find(x)` follows parent links to the root. `union(a, b)` finds both roots and, when they differ, makes one the parent of the other. Keep a counter of groups and lower it on each real merge.

To keep the chains short, attach the smaller tree under the larger one (keep a size for every root) and shorten paths while you climb them (point nodes at their grandparent or at the root). Without this, a run of unions makes `find` O(n).
explanation:
**The idea.** Give every element a parent pointer. An element that is its own parent is a *root*, and the root names the group. `find(x)` climbs parents up to the root. `union(a, b)` finds both roots and, if they differ, makes one root the parent of the other: two trees become one and the group count drops by one. If the roots are the same, nothing changes and `union` returns `False`.

**Two small changes make it fast.** Without them a run of unions can build one long chain, and every `find` has to walk it: O(n). *Union by size* hangs the smaller tree under the larger one, so trees stay shallow (depth at most log n). *Path compression* (here "path halving": point each node on the way up at its grandparent) flattens the tree as a side effect of every `find`. Together they make every operation almost constant time.

**Why the tests look like they do.** One test joins 0-1, 1-2, ... and then looks up the start of the chain 400,000 times. Another joins 20,000 pairs among 40,000 elements, which punishes keeping an array of group labels and relabelling it on every union.

**What it is for.** Counting connected components (union every edge, then read `component_count()`), finding the edge that closes a cycle (the first `union` that returns `False`), and Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.

**Follow-up.** Add `size_of(x)`, the size of the group that contains `x`. The sizes are already there.
